title: member-notifications job fails for EVERY tenant on EVERY run (cold Redis client) and reports success
what: `sendMemberNotifications()` constructs a brand-new `RedisService` at line 138 and then immediately enters the per-tenant loop. The first statement of `notifyOneTenant` (line 188) is `await plans.getBool(ctx.id, 'email_notifications_enabled')`, a Redis GET. `RedisService` (apps/api/src/platform/redis.service.ts:27) sets `enableOfflineQueue: false`, so any command issued while the socket is still in `connecting` state rejects synchronously with `Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false`. Because each iteration throws on its very first await, the whole loop drains in microseconds — long before the socket reaches `ready`. Every tenant lands in the `catch` at line 159 (`failed++`, a `logger.warn`), and the job then returns a success-shaped JobResult.
impact: Due-soon reminders, overdue notices and hold-ready pickup emails are never sent for any library, on any hourly tick, forever — while the worker's /healthz reports `{"member-notifications":{"ok":true,"message":"N tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due"}}`. For a launch whose selling point is library member notifications, the feature is 100% dead on arrival and the health surface actively says it is fine. Libraries discover it weeks later when patrons complain they were never told a hold was ready.
evidence:
RAN. Isolated stack (Postgres 16 on :55441, Redis on :6391), three seeded tenants, tenant DBs healthy. Invoking the exact registry handler five times:
```
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=reltwo: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=relthree: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=relfour: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
RUN 0: {"dueSoon":0,"overdue":0,"holdReady":0,"tenantsScanned":3,"tenantsFailed":3} 3 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due
```
5/5 runs, 3/3 tenants, zero successes. Separately confirmed the mechanism directly:
```
status right after construct: connecting
immediate get THREW: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false
status after 500ms: ready
later get -> null
```
fix: Await readiness before using a freshly-constructed client: add `async ready(){ if (this.client.status !== 'ready') await new Promise((r,j)=>{this.client.once('ready',r); this.client.once('error',j);}); }` to RedisService and `await redis.ready()` right after line 138 (same for stripe-retry.job.ts:67). Better: pass the worker's long-lived `sharedRedis` into `JobContext` (jobs.types.ts) instead of letting each job mint its own client. Independently, add a regression test that runs the handler against a real Redis without pre-warming.
verification: RE-EXECUTED end to end, not just re-read. (1) Isolated the mechanism: instantiated the real RedisService and issued a GET on the next tick -> `status right after ctor: connecting` / `GET REJECTED -> Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false`, twice in a row. (2) Ran the real handler against the live audit control plane (49 active tenants): every tenant logged `member notifications failed for tenant=<slug>: Stream isn't writeable...` and the function returned `{"message":"49 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due","counts":{"dueSoon":0,"overdue":0,"holdReady":0,"tenantsScanned":49,"tenantsFailed":49}}`. 100% failure, success-shaped message. (3) Checked for a guard elsewhere and found none: EffectivePlanService.readCache (effective-plan.service.ts:275-277) issues the GET with no try/catch, and getEffectivePlan calls it before settings.billingEnabled(), so BILLING_ENABLED=false does not short-circuit the Redis hit. The existing member-notifications.job.spec.ts does not catch this because it supplies a mocked Redis. Severity stands: the feature is 100% dead on every tick.

title: A Redis outage takes down 100% of the API — including /healthz, /readyz and /metrics
what: `SystemModeMiddleware` is applied with `forRoutes('*')` (app.module.ts:118-127). Its `ALWAYS_PASS` list contains `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics`, but the bypass branch still executes `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal()` (line 100) before calling `next()`. `resolveGlobal` → `readCache` (service line 231) → `this.redis.client.get(key)`. With `enableOfflineQueue: false` that rejects the moment Redis is unreachable, the rejection escapes the middleware, and the global filter turns it into a 500. There is no Redis-failure fallback anywhere in the mode resolver, and no in-process cache of the last known mode.
impact: Redis is a hard single point of failure for the entire product, and the failure is not graceful: every route returns HTTP 500 with a support code, the liveness probe reports 500, and the readiness probe reports 500 instead of its designed 503+diagnostics. Redis runs with `mem_limit: 512m` and no `maxmemory` (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:365-370), so a cgroup OOM-kill, an AOF rewrite stall, or a plain `docker restart redis` is a total outage of a library-management system in the middle of a circulation desk shift. Staff cannot check a book out; the readiness signal cannot tell an operator why.
evidence:
RAN. API booted against an isolated Redis, then `redis-cli -p 6391 shutdown nosave`:
```
healthz: 500
readyz : {"statusCode":500,...,"supportCode":"D72JZ1WC"} [500]
/auth/me   500
/t/reltwo/catalog/books?take=5   500
login      500
metrics    500
```
Server-side log line for D72JZ1WC: `"url":"/readyz","message":"Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false","stack":"...at SystemModeService.readCache (...)"`. Recovery is automatic: 2 s after restarting Redis, healthz=200 and /auth/me=200.
fix: Two changes. (1) In the `ALWAYS_PASS` branch, do not resolve the mode at all — or wrap it: `req.systemMode = await this.modes.resolveGlobal().catch(() => NORMAL_MODE)`. (2) Make `SystemModeService.readCache/writeCache` fail-open: catch Redis errors, fall through to the control-plane query, and keep a short in-process memo (5–10 s) so a Redis outage degrades to a DB read rather than a 500. Add an integration test that kills Redis and asserts /healthz stays 200 and reads still serve.
verification: Mechanism REPRODUCED exactly, severity reduced. Booted the real API (apps/api/src/main.ts) against the audit stack, then `redis-cli -p 6390 shutdown nosave`: /healthz -> 500, /readyz -> 500 (generic supportCode envelope, NOT the designed 503+dependencies body), /metrics -> 500, /system-mode/current -> 500. Confirmed the cited line: app.module.ts:118-128 applies SystemModeMiddleware with forRoutes('*') and no exclusion, and the ALWAYS_PASS branch (middleware.ts:100) awaits resolveGlobal() before next(). BROADER THAN REPORTED: I also flushed Redis and stopped Postgres, and /healthz still returned 500 — because with a cold mode cache resolveGlobal falls through to `controlDb.systemModeEvent.findFirst`. Liveness therefore depends on BOTH dependencies, not just Redis. DOWNGRADED from blocker to high because the stated harm is bounded and self-correcting: I measured full recovery with no intervention and no restart within ~2 s of Redis returning (healthz=200, readyz=200); there is no data loss and no wedged process; and total unavailability while Redis is down is inherent to this architecture anyway — TenantResolverService (tenant-resolver.service.ts:95-107) and EffectivePlanService have no DB fallback either, so no request path would survive regardless. The genuinely fixable defect is the absence of fail-open on the probes and the mode resolver, which is a serious diagnosability failure, not a launch blocker.

title: Every session cookie is written verbatim into the API's INFO logs — harvested tokens authenticate
what: The pino redact list is `['req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie']` — request headers only. pino-http serialises the response with `pino-std-serializers.res`, which returns `{statusCode, headers: res.getHeaders()}`. `set-cookie` is therefore logged in full on every response that mints a session: `/auth/login`, `/auth/signup`, admin login, impersonation redemption, and every sliding-session refresh.
impact: The API's stdout — captured by Docker's json-file driver, 50 MB × 5 files per container (docker-compose.prod.yml:118-123) — is a rolling store of live, unexpired session JWTs (default remember-me TTL is 30 days). Anyone who can read container logs (host shell, a log shipper, a support bundle, an operator screenshot) can take over any account that logged in during the retention window, including tenant owners and platform admins. No credential, no MFA, no re-auth.
evidence:
RAN. Signed up a tenant against a live API, then grepped its own log file:
```
"set-cookie":"libriant_session=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJjbXQ1bWx4emowMDAwOXltdjJtM2pxdmMyIiwidGlkIjoi..."
```
Replaying that exact token straight from the log file:
```
curl -H "Cookie: libriant_session=$TOK" .../auth/me  ->  HTTP=200
{"user":{"id":"cmt5mlxzj00009ymv2m3jqvc2","email":"rel@example.com","role":"owner"},...}
```
Also confirmed the serializer independently: `pino-std-serializers.res(fakeRes)` → `{"statusCode":null,"headers":{"set-cookie":["lbr_session=..."],...}}`.
fix: Extend the redact paths to cover the response and every cookie name: `redact: { paths: ['req.headers.authorization','req.headers.cookie','res.headers["set-cookie"]'], censor: '[redacted]' }`. Belt and braces: supply a custom `serializers.res` that emits only `statusCode` and `content-length`. Rotate/purge existing logs on any host that has run this build.
verification: RE-EXECUTED. Two independent checks. (1) Serializer: `pino-std-serializers@7.1.0 .res()` on a fake response returns `{"statusCode":null,"headers":{"set-cookie":[...],...}}` — set-cookie is in the serialised object. (2) Live API: POST /auth/logout, then read the API's own log file. The pino-http INFO line contains `"res":{"statusCode":204,"headers":{...,"set-cookie":"libriant_session=; Path=/; ..."}}`. The logout cookie is empty by construction, but it proves the response Set-Cookie header is emitted verbatim into stdout, so a login/signup response logs the live JWT. Verified the cited guard does NOT cover it: app.module.ts:48 `redact: ['req.headers.authorization','req.headers.cookie']` — request headers only, no res path. Severity stands (note: this is a credential-exposure finding sitting in the reliability set; dedupe against authn-authz if it also appears there).

title: No alert is ever delivered to a human — Alertmanager is commented out and the monitoring stack is not part of any deploy
what: prometheus.yml's `alerting:`/`alertmanagers:` block is commented out, and alerts.yml's own header states the rules are only "visible in the Prometheus + Grafana 'Alerts' views" until one is wired. There is no Alertmanager service in infra/monitoring/docker-compose.monitoring.yml's scrape/alert path and no email/Slack/ntfy receiver anywhere in the repo. The monitoring stack is a separate manual `docker compose -f infra/monitoring/docker-compose.monitoring.yml up -d` (docs/deployment-hetzner.md:790) that no deploy step, script, or workflow runs.
impact: `LibriantApiDown`, `HostDiskCritical`, `LibriantPgConnectionsCritical` — none of them reach a person. Nobody wakes up at 3am because nothing wakes them. Compounding this, Compose's `restart: unless-stopped` does not act on healthcheck failures, so a container that is up-but-permanently-unhealthy (the Redis-outage state in reliability-02, a wedged queue consumer) is neither restarted nor reported. On Monday the detection path for a total outage is 'a librarian emails support'.
evidence: READ. `grep -n alertmanagers infra/monitoring/prometheus.yml` → line 19, inside a comment block. alerts.yml lines 5-7: "Wire an Alertmanager (email / Slack / ntfy) in prometheus.yml to actually deliver these; until then they're visible in the Prometheus + Grafana 'Alerts' views." `grep -rn 'docker-compose.monitoring' .github/ scripts/` → no matches (only two doc mentions).
fix: Before launch: add an Alertmanager container to the monitoring compose file with one receiver the founder actually reads (email to the ops mailbox, or ntfy/Pushover on a phone), uncomment the `alerting:` block, and add the monitoring stack to the deploy runbook's mandatory steps. Also add an external, off-box uptime check (healthchecks.io / UptimeRobot) hitting the public origin, so a dead host — which also kills Prometheus — is still detected.
verification: Re-derived from the files. prometheus.yml:17-21 — the whole `alerting:`/`alertmanagers:` block is commented out; the only live directive is `rule_files: - /etc/prometheus/alerts.yml`. alerts.yml:5-7 states delivery is not wired. `grep -rni alertmanager` over the repo returns only comments in those two files plus server-handbook.md:389 which admits it. alerts.yml defines 10 rules (TargetDown, LibriantApiDown, HostDiskCritical, LibriantPgConnectionsCritical, ...) with no delivery path for any of them. `grep -rn docker-compose.monitoring` finds only its own header comment and two doc lines — no script or workflow starts it. Also verified the compounding claim: docker compose `restart: unless-stopped` does not act on healthcheck state, so an up-but-unhealthy container is neither restarted nor reported. Severity stands: this is the finding that makes several others undetectable.

title: restore.sh untars tenant uploads into the in-container path on the host — a default restore silently recovers zero files and reports success
what: `STORAGE_DIR="${STORAGE_DIR:-/srv/libriant/storage}"`. That is the IN-CONTAINER mount target (docker-compose.prod.yml:168,228 `storage:/srv/libriant/storage`); on the host, uploads live in the `libriant_storage` docker volume. backup.sh went to considerable lengths to fix exactly this asymmetry — it resolves the real mountpoint via `docker volume inspect ... --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'` (backup.sh:54-63) and its own comment states the in-container path "does NOT exist on the host, so defaulting to it silently skipped every upload". restore.sh never got the same treatment. With the default, restore.sh does `mkdir -p /srv/libriant/storage`, untars every tenant's covers/branding/exports into that freshly-created host directory, logs `storage restored`, and finishes with `restore complete`. No container ever mounts it.
impact: During a real recovery — the one time this script is ever run, under pressure — every tenant upload appears to be restored and none of it is. The operator gets a clean exit and a green tenant-count check (which only counts databases), puts the cluster back into service, and the libraries find their cover images, logos and generated exports gone. The correct invocation exists only in prose (docs/server-handbook.md:449, docs/deployment-hetzner.md:661 pass `STORAGE_DIR=/mnt/libriant/storage`); nothing in the script enforces it, and deployment-hetzner.md:620 tells the operator that for backup "no STORAGE_DIR is needed", which primes them to omit it for restore too.
evidence: READ. `scripts/restore.sh:30` `STORAGE_DIR="${STORAGE_DIR:-/srv/libriant/storage}"` versus `scripts/backup.sh:54-63` which resolves `docker volume inspect "${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME}_storage" --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'` with fallbacks and then hard-aborts if the directory is missing. The DR drill does not exercise storage at all (see reliability-08), so nothing catches the divergence.
fix: Copy backup.sh's resolution block into restore.sh verbatim (volume inspect → conventional volume path → bind path) and make an unresolvable/nonexistent STORAGE_DIR a hard `die`, not a silent `mkdir -p`. After untarring, assert a non-zero file count and print the resolved path. Add a storage round-trip leg to dr-drill.sh.
verification: Re-derived, and I closed the one gap the original evidence left open — whether /srv/libriant/storage happens to be a host path after all. It is not: docker-compose.prod.yml:401-407 declares `storage:` as a NAMED VOLUME (the file's own header says 'The single bind mount is the storage box' but the volumes block lists storage among pg_data/redis_data/caddy_*), so the host path is /var/lib/docker/volumes/<project>_storage/_data and /srv/libriant/storage exists only inside the containers. restore.sh:30 defaults to the in-container path and restore.sh:145-161 does `mkdir -p "$STORAGE_DIR"` then `tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR" -xzf` and logs `storage restored` — no existence check, no post-untar file-count assertion. backup.sh:50-56 does resolve the real mountpoint via `docker volume inspect` with two fallbacks, and backup.sh:139-147 HARD ABORTS on a missing dir; restore.sh has neither. Confirmed the doc asymmetry that primes the mistake: deployment-hetzner.md:620 'no STORAGE_DIR needed' for backup vs :661 and server-handbook.md:449 which pass STORAGE_DIR for restore. Severity stands — this is a silent total-loss-of-uploads path on the one run that matters.

title: Scheduled jobs report success while every tenant fails — tenantsFailed is discarded by the runner
what: Each multi-tenant sweep catches per-tenant errors, increments a local `failed` counter, emits a `logger.warn`, and then builds its `JobResult` with a message that never mentions failures and a `counts.tenantsFailed` field. The runner (line 92) stores only `{ at, message: result.message, ok: true }` in `lastResults` — `result.counts` is dropped entirely. jobs.types.ts documents counts as something that "get bumped on `libriant_worker_jobs_total{job=...}` later"; that metric does not exist — the worker's /metrics (worker.ts:110-135) exposes only uptime and in-flight gauges.
impact: The one health surface an operator would look at — the worker's /healthz `scheduledLastResults` — actively lies. A tenant whose fine accrual, reservation-pickup expiry, storage cleanup or member notifications throw on every tick shows up as `"ok": true, "message": "3 tenant(s) scanned; no fines to accrue"`. The only trace is a warn line in a rolling Docker log that nothing alerts on (see reliability-04). Fines silently stop accruing, holds silently stop expiring, and the failure is discovered by a librarian, months later, as a data-integrity complaint.
evidence:
RAN. Pointed one tenant's `dbUrl` at an unreachable host and invoked the handlers directly:
```
WARN [FineAccrualSweeper] accrual failed for tenant=reltwo: 
FINE-ACCRUAL RESULT: {"message":"1 tenant(s) scanned; no fines to accrue","counts":{"fines":0,"tenantsScanned":1,"tenantsFailed":1}}
WARN [MemberNotifications] member notifications failed for tenant=reltwo: ...
MEMBER-NOTIFICATIONS RESULT: {"message":"1 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due","counts":{...,"tenantsScanned":1,"tenantsFailed":1}}
```
100% of tenants failed; both messages read as clean successes. Note also that the fine-accrual warn line carried an EMPTY reason (`... for tenant=reltwo: ` with nothing after the colon), so even the log line does not say what went wrong.
fix: In scheduled-jobs.runner.ts store the whole `JobResult` (message + counts) and set `ok: false` when `counts.tenantsFailed > 0`. Append the failure count to every sweep's message (`… ; N tenant(s) FAILED`). Export `libriant_worker_job_last_ok{job=...}` and `libriant_worker_job_tenants_failed{job=...}` from worker.ts /metrics and add a Prometheus rule on them. Log the full error object, not `(err as Error).message`, so an empty-message Prisma init error still says something.
verification: Confirmed by reading the runner and by my own execution of reliability-01. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:88-99 stores `{ at, message: result.message, ok: true }` — `result.counts` is never read, so tenantsFailed cannot reach lastResults(), which is what /healthz surfaces. My live run of sendMemberNotifications() produced `tenantsFailed: 49` alongside the message '49 tenant(s) scanned; no member reminders due', so the health surface would show ok:true with that text. Verified the missing metric claim: `grep -rn 'requests_total|http_request|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` returns nothing, and a live /metrics scrape returned only uptime, build_info, tenants_total, storage_used_bytes, pg_connections(+max), pg_cache_hit_ratio and redis_used_memory_bytes — no per-job gauge exists. One correction to the finding's framing: fine-accrual.job.ts does not touch Redis at all (`grep -rn 'new RedisService()' apps/api/src` -> worker.ts:161, stripe-retry.job.ts:67, member-notifications.job.ts:138 only), so its failure mode is a genuinely independent one (tenant-DB unreachable) rather than a second instance of reliability-01. The masking defect is the same in both. Severity stands: this is the mechanism that hid reliability-01.

title: A backup that never runs, or aborts every night, is undetectable — the dead-man's switch is optional and unset
what: backup.sh aborts (exit 1) on six distinct conditions: control-DB query failure, an off-host tenant, a <1 KiB dump, a failed gzip integrity check on either archive, and a missing storage dir. All of them write to stdout, which the documented cron redirects to `/var/log/libriant/backup.log`. The only active notification is `BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL`, which is (a) optional, (b) pinged only on SUCCESS at the very end, and (c) not written by ensure-env.sh, not present in .env.prod.example, and not mentioned in the cron line in either doc. Nothing installs the crontab either — it exists only as a comment in backup.sh:21 and a snippet in docs/deployment-hetzner.md:646 and docs/server-handbook.md:427.
impact: On a host where the operator forgot the crontab line, or where the cron silently aborts (a relocated tenant, a full disk truncating the gzip, a wrong STORAGE_DIR), there is simply no backup and no signal. Given reliability-04 (nothing alerts at all), the first time anyone learns the backups stopped is when a restore is needed. For a product holding other organisations' catalogues and member records, that is the top-of-list 3am scenario.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn 'BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL' .` matches only scripts/backup.sh:208-209 — no .env.prod.example entry, no ensure-env.sh write, no doc reference. `grep -rn 'crontab' scripts/ .github/` → no matches; the cron is prose only. backup.sh:208 gates the ping on `[ -n "${BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL:-}" ]`, so unset means silence.
fix: Make the heartbeat mandatory in production: have ensure-env.sh provision `BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL` and have backup.sh refuse to run without it (or log a loud WARN and set a non-zero exit) when NODE_ENV/production markers are present. Ping a `/start` endpoint at the top and `/fail` from an `ERR` trap so aborts are reported, not just successes. Ship the crontab as a file (`infra/cron/libriant-backup`) installed by the deploy script rather than a snippet to copy by hand.
verification: Substance confirmed, one piece of the evidence corrected. backup.sh:206-212: the heartbeat is gated on `[ -n "${BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL:-}" ]` and sits in section '6. Success heartbeat' at the very end, after the rclone push — so it fires only on success, never on any of the aborts. CORRECTION: the finding says grep matches only backup.sh; it also matches scripts/secrets.ts:292-304, where BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL IS catalogued — but with `requirement: 'optional'` and `gen: { kind: 'none' }`, so nothing provisions or demands it. Everything else holds: it is absent from .env.prod.example (which has RCLONE_REMOTE= empty at :101 but no heartbeat line), absent from ensure-env.sh, and `grep -rn 'crontab|cron.d' scripts/ .github/` returns a single hit — a comment at backup.sh:20. deploy-on-host.sh checks docker, data dirs, cert and admin email but never that the backup cron exists. Combined with reliability-04 (no alert delivery at all), a backup that never runs is genuinely undetectable. Severity stands — for a product holding other organisations' member records this is the top-of-list 3am scenario.

title: The documented 'prove the restore works' drill still uses the pre-fix, unfiltered pipeline — aimed at the live cluster
what: Under the heading "Before you need it: prove the restore works", the guide instructs: `rclone copy "$BACKUP_REMOTE:$(date -d yesterday +%Y%m%d)" .` then `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U libriant -d postgres`. That is precisely the pipeline the 2026-08-22 fix exists to replace: no `pg_restore_preamble`, no `pg_restore_filter` (scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh), and it targets 127.0.0.1 — the production cluster — despite the surrounding prose claiming it restores "into a throwaway database". `$BACKUP_REMOTE` is also not a variable this repo defines (backup.sh uses `RCLONE_REMOTE`), so the copy step fails and the operator improvises.
impact: An operator following the guide's own pre-launch checklist pipes a `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists` script — which begins with `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS` for every database — straight into the live cluster. Without `ON_ERROR_STOP` it does not abort cleanly; it grinds through partial drops, failed creates against still-connected databases, and duplicate-key errors re-importing over live tables. The single documented step called 'prove the restore works' is itself a production-destroying command. It also teaches the wrong pipeline, so the operator will reach for it again during an actual incident.
evidence: READ. docs/deployment-hetzner.md:874-882 quoted above. Contrast scripts/restore.sh:127-131, which wraps the same stream as `{ pg_restore_preamble "$PG_ROLE"; gunzip -c ... | pg_restore_filter "$PG_ROLE"; } | psql ... -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, and scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh:9-18 which records that the unfiltered form "destroys everything and restores nothing. Reproduced: psql exit 3, zero databases left." The correct procedure does exist two hundred lines earlier in the same file (deployment-hetzner.md:650-662, which calls restore.sh) — this second copy was never updated.
fix: Delete the raw-psql snippet and replace it with `bash scripts/dr-drill.sh` (against a throwaway cluster) plus `STORAGE_DIR=... BACKUP_ROOT=... scripts/restore.sh <YYYYMMDD> --yes` on a rebuilt host. Grep the whole docs/ tree for any other `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql` occurrence and remove it.
verification: The snippet is exactly as quoted (deployment-hetzner.md:872-882: `rclone copy "$BACKUP_REMOTE:..."` then `gunzip -c *.sql.gz | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U libriant -d postgres`), and $BACKUP_REMOTE is indeed undefined anywhere in the repo — `grep -rn 'BACKUP_REMOTE\|RCLONE_REMOTE' scripts/ docs/` shows backup.sh:41 uses RCLONE_REMOTE. But the stated impact does NOT follow. I checked whether that psql can reach production: it cannot. In docker-compose.prod.yml the ONLY service with a `ports:` mapping is caddy (lines 135-138, 80/443); postgres (305-334) and pgbouncer (336-360) are on the internal `data` network with no published port, and the file's own network comment at 389-391 says the data tier 'CANNOT publish'. `psql -h 127.0.0.1` on the host gets connection refused — there is no live cluster on the host loopback to destroy. The rclone step also fails first on the undefined variable. So the real defect is narrower: the documented pre-launch 'prove the restore works' procedure is broken and teaches the unfiltered pipeline that scripts/_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh exists to prevent, leaving the operator with no working drill and a dangerous pattern to improvise from (it WOULD destroy if they reached for `dc exec -T postgres psql` when 127.0.0.1 refused). Downgraded high -> medium: documentation defect with a plausible but indirect path to harm, not a production-destroying command as written.

title: The DR drill passes, but it covers only Postgres — storage, backup.sh, restore.sh and the off-site copy are all untested
what: I re-ran the drill and it is sound (see evidence). What it does not cover: (a) the storage tarball — backup.sh's `tar -C "$STORAGE_DIR"` and restore.sh's untar are never exercised, which is exactly why reliability-05 survived; (b) backup.sh itself — the drill re-implements only `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists | gzip -9`, so the off-host-tenant guard, the volume-mountpoint resolution, the prune, the manifest and the rclone push are untested; (c) restore.sh itself — the drill imports `_lib/pg-restore-filter.sh` but never invokes restore.sh, so the container stop/start ordering, the `trap restart_apps EXIT`, the archive validation and the tenant-count assertion are untested; (d) the off-site leg — nothing ever pulls a backup back from `RCLONE_REMOTE`; (e) realism — the fixture is 502 rows and a 5 KB dump, so nothing about restore duration or RTO is known; (f) restoring an OLD dump against NEWER code, i.e. Prisma migration drift after a rollback.
impact: The repo's stated guarantee — "scripts/dr-drill.sh now proves it" — is narrower than it reads. A green drill is compatible with a recovery that loses every uploaded file (reliability-05), with a backup that never ran (reliability-09), and with an off-site copy nobody can actually retrieve. The one leg that is proven is the one that was already fixed.
evidence: RAN. On a purpose-built isolated Postgres 16 cluster (`initdb --auth-host=scram-sha-256`, port 55441): `30 checks passed, 0 failed / DR DRILL PASSED — backup → restore round trip is sound` in 3.4 s, including the negative control `✓ password auth is enforced`, `✓ self-role drift undone`, `✓ role can still authenticate`, row censuses, extension sets, sequence values and byte-identical schema diffs for all three fixture databases. Coverage gaps confirmed by reading: `grep -n 'storage\|restore.sh\|backup.sh' scripts/dr-drill.sh` matches only comments and the re-implemented `pg_dumpall` line at 210.
fix: Extend the drill: create a fixture storage tree, run the real `backup.sh` (with COMPOSE overrides pointed at the fixture) and the real `restore.sh --yes` against the throwaway target, then diff the storage tree and assert file count/checksums. Add an `rclone` round-trip leg against a local `rclone` remote. Record and print elapsed restore time so RTO is a measured number.
verification: Coverage claim CONFIRMED by grep: `grep -n 'storage|restore.sh|backup.sh|rclone' scripts/dr-drill.sh` matches only header comments plus line 209-210, which re-implements `pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists | gzip -9` inline. The script sources _lib/pg-restore-filter.sh but never invokes backup.sh or restore.sh, and there is no storage tarball leg and no rclone leg. Worth adding: the CI step that runs it (.github/workflows/verify.yml:338-341) describes itself as exercising 'the real backup.sh -> restore.sh pipeline', which is the same overstatement. Downgraded high -> medium because the harm is entirely derivative: the concrete defects the gap allows through are reliability-05 (storage restore) and reliability-09 (unmonitored backup), both reported separately at high. On its own, a narrow drill causes no failure — it only fails to catch one. Rating it high alongside its own consequences double-counts the same 3am event.

title: Abandoned ('dead') outbox emails have no surface anywhere — password resets can be dropped silently
what: After `maxAttempts` the worker writes `status: 'dead', abandonedAt: now, lastError: reason` and gives up. Repo-wide, the only other reads of `'dead'` are the skip check at line 175 — there is no admin endpoint, no metric, no /healthz field, no scheduled sweep and no alert that counts dead rows. The single trace is one `console.error` per failure in a rolling Docker log.
impact: When the provider is misconfigured, rate-limits, or a domain gets blocked, password-reset links, email-verification links and hold-ready notices are permanently abandoned with no operator-visible signal. Users experience 'the reset email never arrives' and support has no way to see it happened, let alone re-drive it. This becomes live the moment EMAIL_DRIVER stops being `console`.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn "'dead'" apps/api/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v spec` → exactly two hits, both in email-worker.ts (175, 215). `grep -rn 'emailOutbox' apps/api/src | grep -v email-worker\|email.service` → one hit, an unrelated read in support-session-expiry.job.ts:71. No admin route, no metric.
fix: Expose `libriant_email_outbox_rows{status=...}` from the worker's /metrics and add a Prometheus rule on `dead > 0` and on `pending` older than N minutes. Add an admin panel view of the outbox with a re-drive action (set back to `pending`, reset attempts), so a provider outage is recoverable rather than a permanent data loss of user-facing mail.
verification: Mechanism confirmed: `grep -rn "'dead'" apps/api/src --include='*.ts' | grep -v spec` returns exactly two hits, email-worker.ts:175 (skip) and :215 (write). Files touching emailOutbox at all: email-worker.ts, email.service.ts, support-session-expiry.job.ts — no admin route, no metric, no healthz field. Downgraded high -> medium after reading the surrounding code: the failure is not actually silent at the point it happens. email-worker.ts:219 re-throws after marking the row, so BullMQ records the failure and the worker's failed handler logs it; the row itself is durable and carries `lastError`, `failedAt` and `abandonedAt`, so a dead letter is recoverable by SQL rather than lost; and the triggering condition (a misconfigured or blocked provider) fails EVERY message, which is loud in logs. What is genuinely missing is an operator surface and a re-drive action, which is an observability gap of the same family as reliability-04/17 rather than an independent high. Note the finding is correct that this is dormant only while EMAIL_DRIVER=console.

title: /readyz's dependency breakdown never reaches the caller — the global filter re-skins the 503 into a generic envelope
what: The readiness handler deliberately builds `{status:'not_ready', dependencies:{redis, controlDb}}` and throws it inside a `ServiceUnavailableException`. `HttpExceptionFilter` treats any status >= 500 — 503 included — as a server bug: it discards the declared body, mints a support code, logs the whole thing, and returns the generic "Sorry — something went wrong on our end… code: XXXXXXXX" envelope.
impact: The one endpoint designed to tell an operator WHICH dependency is down tells them nothing. `docker inspect` shows `unhealthy` with a useless body, a `wget -qO- /readyz` gives a support code instead of `{"redis":true,"controlDb":false}`, and diagnosis requires grepping the API log for that code. It also means every failed readiness probe (every 15 s per the compose healthcheck) writes a full stack trace, so a DB outage floods the log with 4 stack traces a minute.
evidence:
RAN. With Postgres stopped and Redis up:
```
readyz: {"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end. We've logged it. Please try again, or send us this code if it keeps happening: 784L88W5","supportCode":"784L88W5"} [503]
```
The designed body `{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{...}}` is nowhere in the response.
fix: Either exempt 503 from the re-skin (`if (status < 500 || status === HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE) { res.status(status).json(body); return; }`), or have the readiness handler write the response directly with `@Res()` instead of throwing. Also drop the readiness probe's log level from `error`+stack to a single warn line so a DB outage does not bury the real errors.
verification: RE-EXECUTED against the live API. Stopped Postgres with Redis up (so the readiness handler itself ran) and got: `{"statusCode":503,"error":"InternalServerError","message":"Sorry — something went wrong on our end... code: 4FWVPCBI","supportCode":"4FWVPCBI"}` with HTTP 503. The designed body `{"status":"not_ready","dependencies":{"redis":...,"controlDb":...}}` from health.controller.ts:41-47 is nowhere in the response. Cause re-read and confirmed: http-exception.filter.ts:44-49 passes through only `status < 500`, so 503 falls into handle5xx (lines 76-105), which discards `declaredBody`, mints a support code and logs a full stack. The log-flood sub-claim also holds — the compose healthcheck polls /readyz every 15 s (docker-compose.prod.yml:223-228), so a DB outage writes four stack traces a minute. Severity stands.

title: The stripe-retry sweep has the same cold-Redis defect, and it only bites when there is something to retry
what: Identical shape to reliability-01: `const redis = new RedisService()` at line 67, then the first thing the loop does is `await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', ..., 'NX')` at line 88 on a socket that is still `connecting`, which rejects under `enableOfflineQueue:false`. Unlike member-notifications, that throw is not caught per-row — it escapes the whole handler, so the sweep aborts having retried nothing. The job returns early (`if (failed.length === 0) return`) whenever there is nothing to do, so the bug is invisible on a healthy system and fires exactly when failed Stripe webhook events exist.
impact: Currently dormant (BILLING_ENABLED=false, STRIPE_DRIVER=fake). The moment billing is switched on, the safety net for failed Stripe webhooks — the thing that stops a missed `customer.subscription.updated` from leaving a library on the wrong plan or wrongly suspended — fails on its first event every 5 minutes. At least this one is loud: BullMQ marks the job failed and the runner records `ok:false`.
evidence: READ, mechanism proven by execution elsewhere. Same construct-then-immediately-command pattern as member-notifications.job.ts:138/188, whose failure I reproduced 5/5 times (reliability-01). stripe-retry.job.ts:67 `const redis = new RedisService();`, line 88 `const claimed = await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', SWEEP_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS, 'NX');` with no intervening await that yields long enough for the socket to reach `ready`.
fix: Same as reliability-01 — `await redis.ready()` after construction, or take the shared client from JobContext. Fix both call sites together; `grep -rn 'new RedisService()' apps/api/src` finds all three (worker.ts:161 is the correct, long-lived one).
verification: UPGRADED FROM read-only TO EXECUTED. I inserted a failed webhook row into the live control plane (`stripeWebhookEvent { id: 'evt_audit_rel16', type: 'customer.subscription.updated', error: 'previous failure' }`) and invoked sweepFailedStripeWebhooks() directly. Result: `SWEEP THREW: Stream isn't writeable and enableOfflineQueue options is false` — the whole handler aborts on the first row, retrying nothing, exactly as predicted. Re-read confirms the cited lines: stripe-retry.job.ts:67 `const redis = new RedisService()` and :88 `await redis.client.set(lockKey, '1', 'EX', SWEEP_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS, 'NX')`, with the early return at :61 hiding it whenever there is nothing to retry. Severity stands at medium: dormant while BILLING_ENABLED=false, and unlike reliability-01 it is loud when it fires (the throw escapes, BullMQ marks the job failed, the runner records ok:false).

title: The API exports no request, error or latency metrics — a 5xx storm is unalertable
what: `/metrics` emits `libriant_api_uptime_seconds`, `libriant_api_build_info`, tenant counts by status, summed storage bytes, Postgres connection count/max, Postgres cache-hit ratio and Redis used_memory. There is no HTTP request counter, no status-code breakdown, no latency histogram, and no per-tenant error counter. The worker's /metrics is similarly limited to uptime plus in-flight gauges. Consequently infra/monitoring/alerts.yml has no rule that could reference an error rate.
impact: There is no signal for 'the app is up but broken'. A regression that 500s one route, a tenant whose every request errors, a latency cliff after a bad migration — all invisible to Prometheus and Grafana. The only availability signal is `up{job="libriant-api"}`, which requires /metrics itself to fail. Reliability-02 happens to trip that (Redis down 500s /metrics too), but a narrower breakage will not.
evidence: READ, and RAN. Full scrape of a live API returned only the gauges listed above. `grep -n 'requests_total\|http_request\|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` → no matches. infra/monitoring/alerts.yml contains no rule mentioning an error or request metric.
fix: Add a tiny counter/histogram in the pino-http `onResponse` hook or a global interceptor: `libriant_api_requests_total{method,route,status}` and `libriant_api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route}`. Then add alert rules for sustained 5xx ratio and p95 latency. Route labels must be the Nest route pattern, not the raw URL, so tenant slugs and ids do not explode cardinality.
verification: RE-EXECUTED. Full scrape of the live API's /metrics returned exactly eight gauges and nothing else: libriant_api_uptime_seconds, libriant_api_build_info, libriant_tenants_total{status}, libriant_storage_used_bytes, libriant_pg_connections, libriant_pg_connections_max, libriant_pg_cache_hit_ratio, libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes. `grep -rn 'requests_total|http_request|_duration_seconds' apps/api/src` -> no matches. Cross-checked the consequence: `grep -n 'alert:' infra/monitoring/alerts.yml` lists 10 rules (TargetDown, LibriantApiDown, HostLowMemory, HostSwapping, HostDiskFilling, HostDiskCritical, HostHighCPU, LibriantPgConnectionsHigh, LibriantPgConnectionsCritical, LibriantPgCacheHitLow) — every one is a liveness or host/DB-capacity rule; none can express an error rate or latency. The 'up but broken' state is genuinely unobservable. Severity stands.

title: An aborted dr-drill.sh leaves the shared superuser role crippled (statement_timeout=1s, CONNECTION LIMIT 7)
what: The drill deliberately drifts the restoring role — `ALTER ROLE $PGUSER CONNECTION LIMIT 7; ALTER ROLE $PGUSER SET statement_timeout = '1s';` (lines 218-219) — so the post-restore assertions cannot be tautologies. The undo lives only in the 'Cleaning up' block at the very end of a successful run. The EXIT trap (line 47) is `trap 'restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT`, and `restore_password` issues only `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD`. Any abort after line 219 — `set -e` on a failed psql, a Ctrl-C, a lock wait, a concurrent process dropping a database mid-`pg_dumpall` — leaves the role with a 1-second statement timeout and a 7-connection cap.
impact: The whole stack authenticates as this one role. A cluster left in that state fails every query longer than a second and refuses the 8th connection: the API's Prisma pools, pgbouncer's server pool and the worker's per-tenant clients all break, and the symptom (`canceling statement due to statement timeout`, `too many connections for role`) points nowhere near a shell script that exited an hour ago. The script's only guard is the comment 'Never point it at production'.
evidence:
RAN, unintentionally — which is the point. My first drill invocation aborted mid-run (a concurrent process dropped a tenant database during `pg_dumpall`). Immediately afterwards, on that cluster:
```
psql -qtAX -c "SELECT rolname, rolconnlimit, rolconfig FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='libriant'"
libriant|7|{statement_timeout=1s}
```
I had to repair it by hand with `ALTER ROLE libriant RESET ALL; ALTER ROLE libriant WITH CONNECTION LIMIT -1`.
fix: Move the role reset into the EXIT trap: `trap 'undo_drift; restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT`, where `undo_drift` runs `ALTER ROLE "$PGUSER" RESET ALL; ALTER ROLE "$PGUSER" WITH CONNECTION LIMIT -1 VALID UNTIL 'infinity'`. Additionally refuse to start when the target cluster contains a `libriant_control` database (a production fingerprint) unless `--i-know-this-is-not-production` is passed.
verification: Mechanism confirmed exactly: dr-drill.sh:47 `trap 'restore_password; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT` and restore_password (lines 38-46) issues only `ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD`; the drift at lines 217-220 sets `CONNECTION LIMIT 7` and `statement_timeout = '1s'` and is undone only by the successful restore later in the run, not by the trap. Any abort in between leaves the role crippled. Downgraded medium -> low on blast radius. This script is explicitly a throwaway-cluster tool: its header (lines 30-31) says 'DESTRUCTIVE: drops and recreates its own fixture databases... Never point it at production', and its only automated caller (.github/workflows/verify.yml:341-352) runs it against a dedicated postgres service container on port 5433, deliberately separated from the shared 5432 service. The impact paragraph describes production Prisma pools and pgbouncer breaking, which requires an operator to have aimed a self-described production-destroying script at production. Real defect (the trap should undo the drift, and a `libriant_control` fingerprint check is a cheap guard), but it is developer-tooling hygiene, not a launch reliability risk.

title: Library errors carrying a 4xx status are returned to the client with zero logging
what: Path 1.5 inspects any non-HttpException for a numeric `status`/`statusCode` in 400-499 and, if found, responds with that status and a canned message — and returns without a single log call. The intent is body-parser's `PayloadTooLargeError`/`SyntaxError`, but the shape is generic: Stripe's SDK errors carry `statusCode`, http-errors and most HTTP client wrappers carry `status`, and any of them thrown from a handler now produces a client-visible 4xx with no server-side record.
impact: A whole class of upstream failures becomes invisible: no support code, no log line, no metric. If the Stripe API starts returning 402/429, or the GitHub desktop-release proxy starts 404ing, the user sees "We couldn't process that request" and the operator has literally nothing to correlate — not even a count. Silent 4xx is the hardest failure mode to notice, and this path guarantees it.
evidence: READ. apps/api/src/platform/http-exception.filter.ts:63-72 — between `const clientStatus = clientErrorStatus(exception)` and `return`, there is no `this.logger.*` call, unlike both other branches which route through `handle5xx` and its single-line JSON log.
fix: Log a warn line (method, url, status, error message, constructor name) before responding on this path, and narrow the trigger: only honour the status when the exception is an instance of an expected body-parser/http-errors type (`err.type === 'entity.too.large'` / `'entity.parse.failed'`), letting everything else fall through to the 5xx path where it gets a support code and a stack.
verification: Mechanism confirmed: http-exception.filter.ts:63-70, between `clientErrorStatus(exception)` and the `return`, contains no logger call, and `clientErrorStatus` (lines 116-121) is indeed generic — it accepts any object with a numeric `status` or `statusCode` in 400-499, which does match Stripe SDK errors and http-errors. Downgraded medium -> low because the stated impact overreaches. 'The operator has literally nothing to correlate — not even a count' is false: pino-http autologging records every response, and I confirmed on the live API that a 404 produced an INFO line carrying method, url and `"res":{"statusCode":404,...}`. So 4xx on this path are countable and locatable by URL; what is lost is the exception's message and constructor name. The narrowing half of the fix (only honour the status for known body-parser/http-errors shapes, so a Stripe 402/429 is not mislabelled as user error) is the part that matters, and it is a small, contained defect.

title: No stop_grace_period on api, web or postgres — Docker SIGKILLs them 10 s after SIGTERM
what: `stop_grace_period: 60s` is set for the `worker` service and nowhere else. Every other service — api, web, caddy, postgres, pgbouncer, redis — inherits Docker's 10 s default. The API also has no internal shutdown deadline of its own: main.ts calls `app.enableShutdownHooks()` and relies entirely on Nest's `close()`, in contrast to worker.ts:227-262 which races the drain against an explicit 25 s `SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS`.
impact: Two consequences. (a) Any API request still in flight 10 s after a deploy's SIGTERM is severed mid-write — an import commit, a tenant provision (measured at ~1.2 s for a small library, longer as schemas grow), a large export kickoff. (b) More serious: the official postgres image's STOPSIGNAL is SIGINT, i.e. fast shutdown, which still has to complete a shutdown checkpoint. On a 2 GB-limit Postgres with a dirty buffer pool, a checkpoint that overruns 10 s ends in SIGKILL and the next start is a WAL crash recovery — extra downtime, on the component whose death takes the whole cell with it, at exactly the moment an operator is already doing something stressful.
evidence: READ. `grep -n 'stop_grace_period' infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` → one hit, line 297, under `worker`. main.ts has `app.enableShutdownHooks()` (line 57) and no timer; worker.ts:227 defines `SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS = 25_000` and races it at line 258. Separately RAN: an idle HTTP keep-alive socket does NOT block the API's shutdown (SIGTERM → process exited in 1 s with a live keep-alive agent attached), so the exposure is genuinely in-flight work, not connection draining.
fix: Add `stop_grace_period: 30s` to api and web and `stop_grace_period: 120s` to postgres (and tune `checkpoint_timeout`/`max_wal_size` so a shutdown checkpoint is bounded). Mirror worker.ts's bounded-drain pattern in main.ts: register a SIGTERM handler that races `app.close()` against a ~25 s deadline and then `process.exit`.
verification: Facts confirmed: `grep -n stop_grace_period infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml` returns exactly one hit, line 297 under worker; main.ts:57 calls `app.enableShutdownHooks()` with no deadline while worker.ts:208/220/253 races a 25 s SHUTDOWN_DEADLINE_MS. Downgraded medium -> low after testing the two impact legs. (a) The Postgres-checkpoint leg is the serious one on paper, but I measured a fast shutdown of the seeded audit cluster (49 tenants) from its own log: 'checkpoint starting: shutdown immediate' -> 'checkpoint complete: wrote 1098 buffers (6.7%) ... total=0.048 s'. Two orders of magnitude under the 10 s default at launch scale; the risk is real only as the dataset grows. (b) The in-flight-work leg largely does not apply to the API: the long operations named (import commit, export generation, tenant provisioning) run in the worker, which is the ONE service that already has stop_grace_period: 60s and a bounded internal drain. The finding itself already recorded that idle keep-alive sockets do not block shutdown. Cheap fix, correct diagnosis, but it cannot produce the stated 3am event at this scale.

title: Redis has a 512 MB cgroup ceiling and no maxmemory — an OOM-kill is a full outage
what: The comment explains the deliberate choice not to set `--maxmemory` (an eviction policy could drop live BullMQ job keys), and the command passes `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`, which is inert without a `maxmemory`. But `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` still applies at the cgroup level. Redis therefore has no internal backpressure and no eviction; it grows until the kernel OOM-killer takes the container.
impact: There is no soft landing between 'fine' and 'killed'. And because of reliability-02, a killed Redis is not a degraded cache — it is a 100%-500 API. Growth drivers are real: BullMQ keeps `removeOnComplete: 100-1000` / `removeOnFail: 100-5000` per queue across five queues, plus session-adjacent caches, plus AOF buffers during a rewrite. Recovery is bounded (AOF on a named volume, `restart: unless-stopped`), but the outage window is a hard failure of the whole product.
evidence: READ. docker-compose.prod.yml:361-371 — `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` with `command: ['redis-server','--appendonly','yes','--maxmemory-policy','allkeys-lru']` and no `--maxmemory`. Combined with the executed evidence in reliability-02 that a Redis outage 500s every route including /healthz.
fix: Set `--maxmemory` to ~70% of the cgroup limit with `--maxmemory-policy noeviction` — that turns an OOM-kill into write errors Redis reports and the app can log, instead of a process death, while still never evicting a BullMQ key. Export Redis memory to Prometheus (the gauge already exists: `libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes`) and alert at 70% of the limit. Once reliability-02 is fixed, this drops to a nuisance rather than an outage.
verification: Configuration confirmed verbatim: docker-compose.prod.yml:364 `mem_limit: ${REDIS_MEM_LIMIT:-512m}` with :372 `command: ['redis-server','--appendonly','yes','--maxmemory-policy','allkeys-lru']` and no `--maxmemory`. Downgraded medium -> low on two grounds. (1) I measured actual usage on the audit instance carrying 50 seeded tenants plus BullMQ keys: `libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes 1407120` — 1.4 MB against a 512 MB ceiling, roughly 350x headroom, and the launch cohort is five libraries. The finding asserts growth drivers but quantifies none, and no OOM path is demonstrated. (2) The omission is a deliberate, documented trade-off — lines 365-370 explain that eviction could drop live BullMQ job keys and name the durable sources of truth that make a container OOM recoverable. What survives as a genuine defect is smaller and worth keeping: `--maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` is INERT without a `maxmemory`, so the compose file reads as if a protection is configured when none is, and the existing libriant_redis_used_memory_bytes gauge has no alert rule on it.

title: Scheduled BullMQ jobs are registered with no attempts, so they never retry — contradicting the code's own comment
what: `queue.upsertJobScheduler(j.name, { every: j.intervalMs }, { name: j.name, opts: { removeOnComplete: 100, removeOnFail: 100 } })` — no `attempts`, no `backoff`. BullMQ's default is `attempts: 1`, i.e. no retry. The worker body at line 110 nonetheless re-throws with the comment "re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries". The retry never happens; recovery is only the next scheduled tick.
impact: Small in practice — every registered job is an idempotent periodic sweep, so a transient failure costs one interval. But it matters for the hourly jobs: a 2-second Postgres blip at the top of the hour costs `member-notifications` and `fine-accrual` a full hour, and the comment tells the next maintainer that a retry is happening when it is not.
evidence: READ. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:70-74 (the upsert with no `attempts`), versus line 110 `throw err; // re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries`. Contrast apps/api/src/email/email.service.ts:79-80, which does configure `attempts: this.defaultMaxAttempts` and `backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 30_000 }`.
fix: Add `attempts: 3, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 10_000 }` to the scheduler template opts (capped well under the shortest interval so retries cannot overlap the next tick), or correct the comment to say recovery is the next tick. Pick one — the current state is a comment that lies.
verification: Confirmed by reading both sides. scheduled-jobs.runner.ts:69-74 upserts the scheduler with template opts `{ removeOnComplete: 100, removeOnFail: 100 }` and no `attempts`/`backoff`, so BullMQ's default of attempts:1 applies; runner line 110 nonetheless says `throw err; // re-throw so BullMQ marks the job failed + retries`. The contrast case is real too — email.service.ts configures attempts plus exponential backoff. Severity correctly rated low: every registered job in registry.ts is an idempotent periodic sweep, so the cost of a transient failure is one interval. The finding is honest about that. Kept because the comment actively misinforms the next maintainer.

title: Caddy has no retry budget for its single upstreams — every container recreate is a burst of user-visible 502s
what: Two `reverse_proxy api:3001` blocks set `fail_duration 10s` / `max_fails 3`; the webhook proxy (line 189) and both `reverse_proxy web:3000` blocks (lines 194, 235) set nothing. No block sets `lb_try_duration`, so with a single upstream Caddy makes exactly one attempt and returns 502 on a connection refusal. Worse, once passive health marks the sole upstream unhealthy, Caddy short-circuits every request for the full `fail_duration` even if the upstream came back immediately.
impact: Deploys are manual, single-host, and recreate containers in place — there is no second replica to shift traffic to. Every `docker compose up -d` therefore produces a window where users get raw 502s on the main HTML path (`handle { reverse_proxy web:3000 }`) rather than a brief retry. With `fail_duration 10s` on the API path, a 200 ms restart can be amplified into a 10-second blackout. Cheap to fix and it makes most deploys invisible.
evidence: READ. `grep -n 'lb_try_duration' infra/caddy/Caddyfile` → no matches. `fail_duration 10s` / `max_fails 3` appear only at lines 179-180 and 277-278; lines 189, 194 and 235 are bare `reverse_proxy` directives.
fix: Add `lb_try_duration 10s` and `lb_try_interval 250ms` to the web and api reverse_proxy blocks so Caddy rides out a container restart, and lower `fail_duration` to ~2s (or drop passive health entirely for a single upstream, where it can only hurt).
verification: Confirmed by grep over infra/caddy/Caddyfile: `reverse_proxy` appears at 171 (with fail_duration 10s / max_fails 3 at 179-180), 189 (bare), 194 (bare), 218, 235 (bare) and 273 (with fail_duration/max_fails at 277-278); `lb_try_duration` and `lb_try_interval` appear nowhere. With one upstream and no try budget Caddy makes a single attempt and returns 502 on connection refusal, and passive health on a sole upstream can only short-circuit it. Consistent with the deployment model — single host, manual `docker compose up -d`, no second replica — so a container recreate is user-visible. Severity correctly low: the window is seconds, at a moment the operator chose.

title: Verified good: tenant-DB failure is contained, and Postgres/Redis outages recover automatically
what: Three degradation behaviours I probed and found sound, recorded so they are not re-audited. (a) A tenant whose `dbUrl` points at an unreachable host fails fast and only for that tenant. (b) A Postgres outage leaves /healthz at 200 and correctly fails /readyz, and the API recovers with no restart once Postgres returns. (c) A Redis outage is a full outage (reliability-02) but is also fully self-healing. (d) An idle HTTP keep-alive connection does not block the API's shutdown.
impact: None — this is negative evidence. Useful because it narrows the blast radius: the multi-tenant isolation story holds under a per-tenant database failure, and neither dependency outage leaves the process permanently wedged, so remediation is 'restart the dependency', not 'restart the app'.
evidence: RAN. (a) `UPDATE tenants SET "dbUrl"='postgresql://...@192.0.2.77:5432/tenant_dead'`, cache flushed → `books: 500 in 0.11s`, generic envelope, while `healthz=200 readyz=200`. (b) `pg_ctl -m fast stop` → `healthz: 200`, `readyz: [503]`, tenant reads 500; after restart, at t+3s `readyz=200 me=200 books=200`. (c) Redis restarted → `t+2s healthz=200 me=200`. (d) Node keep-alive agent holding an idle socket, `kill -TERM` → `API exited after 1s`.
fix: No change required. Consider keeping these four probes as a scripted chaos smoke test so the properties stay true.
verification: Kept as negative evidence but CORRECTED — one of its four claims is false as stated. Claim (b), 'a Postgres outage leaves /healthz at 200', holds only while the global system-mode blob is warm in Redis. I flushed Redis and then stopped Postgres, and /healthz returned 500, not 200: with a cold cache SystemModeMiddleware's ALWAYS_PASS branch falls through resolveGlobal() to `controlDb.systemModeEvent.findFirst`. So liveness depends on Postgres as well as Redis, which widens reliability-02 rather than bounding it. Claims (a), (c) and (d) I did not contradict, and I independently re-measured (c): after restarting Redis the API returned healthz=200 and readyz=200 within ~2 s with no restart. The value of this entry — that neither dependency leaves the process permanently wedged, so remediation is 'restart the dependency' — survives, with claim (b) narrowed to 'readyz correctly fails and the API self-heals'.
